lesson.title: Two Conditions at Once: An Introduction to Compound Inequalities
lesson.summary: Learn how compound inequalities combine two inequality statements into one, including the three part between form, and solve one by working on all three parts at once.
lesson.body:
A compound inequality is a statement built from two inequalities joined together, describing a solution set that has to satisfy more than one condition simultaneously or has more than one way of being satisfied. There are two ways these inequalities get joined, using the words and or or, and each one produces a different kind of solution set, which the next two sections cover in detail. This section focuses on a particularly common and compact form of an and compound inequality, sometimes called a three part inequality, where a single quantity is squeezed between two boundary values in one continuous statement.

A three part inequality looks like negative 3 is less than x plus 1, which is less than or equal to 5, all written in a single line. This single statement is really shorthand for two separate conditions joined by and: negative 3 is less than x plus 1, and, at the same time, x plus 1 is less than or equal to 5. Writing it as one three part statement instead of two separate ones works because the middle expression, x plus 1 in this case, is shared by both conditions, and it keeps the notation compact without losing any meaning.

Solving a three part inequality uses the same solving techniques from solving linear inequalities, applied to all three parts of the statement at once rather than to just one expression. Consider negative 3 is less than x plus 1, which is less than or equal to 5. The goal is to isolate x in the middle, so the same operation is applied to the left part, the middle part, and the right part simultaneously. Since the middle expression has a plus 1 attached to x, subtract 1 from all three parts: negative 3 minus 1 is less than x plus 1 minus 1, which is less than or equal to 5 minus 1. This simplifies to negative 4 is less than x, which is less than or equal to 4.

Checking this solution means testing values against the original three part inequality, not the simplified one. Try x equals 0, which should be inside the solution set since negative 4 is less than 0 is less than or equal to 4: substituting gives negative 3 is less than 0 plus 1, which is 1, and 1 is less than or equal to 5, and both parts are true. Try the included boundary x equals 4: substituting gives negative 3 is less than 4 plus 1, which is 5, and 5 is less than or equal to 5, so this boundary works and is correctly included. Try the excluded boundary x equals negative 4: substituting gives negative 3 is less than negative 4 plus 1, which is negative 3, and the statement negative 3 is less than negative 3 is false, so negative 4 is correctly excluded from the solution set, matching the strict less than symbol on that side.

Graphing this kind of solution on a number line uses the same open and closed circle rules from graphing inequalities, applied at both ends of the interval instead of just one. Since negative 4 is excluded, it gets an open circle, and since 4 is included, it gets a closed circle, with shading filling in the entire stretch of the number line between them. This two boundary picture is what separates a compound inequality from the single sided inequalities covered earlier in this unit, and it is exactly the kind of solution set produced by an and compound inequality, the topic explored in full detail next.
